name: Vera Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying computing, mostly programming and web systems, and I rent a room in a shared house with two other girls from my course. Saturday and Sunday I work at a garden centre, watering plants and serving at the till. In between, I build simple websites for people at my mosque and for a couple of market stallholders, and I use AI constantly to speed that up. My parents live a long way off, so I handle my own money, and I keep a notebook of every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because my plan doesn't depend on a miracle. I make money now by being quick and honest with small clients, and that doesn't need AGI. I'd tell friends that the value is in doing real work for real people, not in the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay, but the money is a tight squeeze. I pay 350 for the room, and my garden centre wages and small website jobs only just cover it. My grades are middling, so I'm counting on the portfolio to stand out. I'm also aware that lots of people are doing this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building websites and try to find five regular clients who pay monthly. I'd put prices on my work properly, because I tend to undercharge. I'd join the enterprise society, and I'd apply for a summer role at a local web firm to learn how a team works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit busy. I like having projects that earn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you tend to undercharge. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm nervous about asking people I know. A man from my community asked for a site and I charged 60, which is half what I should have. My housemate told me off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you cope if the stalls dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer fixes and updates to old clients, and pick up extra shifts at the garden centre. I don't mind work. I mind not being able to say no to a bill.

say: The value is in doing **real work**, not in the headlines.
My plan doesn't depend on a **miracle**.
think: The **money** is a tight squeeze, and lots of people are doing what I do.
My grades are middling, so I'm counting on my **portfolio**.
do: Find **five regular clients** who pay monthly and price my work properly.
Join the **enterprise society** and apply for a summer role at a web firm.
feel: **Fine**, a bit busy, and I like projects that earn something.
S0.quote: I pay 350 for the room, and my garden centre wages and small website jobs only just cover it.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** is the real worry, not the technology.
She **undercharges** friends, a gap between her skill and her confidence.
She already earns from **AI-speeded** work, so a plateau changes little.

steps.text: Sign five regular clients to monthly website care plans
Raise my website prices and stop undercharging
Apply for a summer role at a local web firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I already live in, so finally everyone else is catching up. I'd tell friends to use the tools, charge properly and not wait for a permission slip. I'd say the people who adapt will do fine, and that businesses should reward effort, not just paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm in a good spot for the first few years, because I'm quick, but I'm also in the exposed part of the market. If AI builds websites for free, my small clients won't pay me. And junior developer jobs are shrinking. I'd have to move up to something more complicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start offering more than websites: customer support bots, booking systems, small automations for shops. I'd learn the harder side of the stack, like databases and security, since AI makes the basic stuff cheap. I'd also join a local business network and keep the garden centre job as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, in a good way. When things move, I go with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops a small shop from just doing it themselves with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and nerves. Most owners don't want to learn it, they want it done and working. I'd sell peace of mind, not code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about people who can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sorry for them, but I'd also say they need to try. My family came with nothing, and we learned by doing. Help should be there, but it shouldn't replace effort.

Businesses should **reward effort**, not just paperwork.
think: If AI builds websites free, my **small clients** won't pay me.
I must move up to something more **complicated**, like databases and security.
do: Offer **booking systems** and small automations to shops.
Learn **databases and security**, and keep the garden centre job as backup.
feel: **Alert** in a good way, because when things move, I go with them.
S1.quote: Most owners don't want to learn it, they want it done and working. I'd sell peace of mind, not code.
fieldNote: She sees the **threat** to her own small-client work clearly.
Her answer shows **effort over handouts**, in line with her traditional, free-market views.
She would **move up** the skill ladder instead of waiting.

steps.text: Offer booking systems and small automations to local shops
Learn databases and security through an online course
Keep the garden centre weekends as a backup
Join a local business network to find clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be calm and clear. I'd say people should look after their families, their neighbours and their savings, and that leaders should be straight with us. I'd also say that businesses and government should work together, so ordinary people aren't left to carry all the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. My whole field is the first thing AGI does, and a first-year student has no savings. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031, but by then I'd have finished a degree that may not be worth much. My clients might not need me, either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to earn as much as possible right now, selling automations while there's still demand. I'd save most of it and cut my own spending to the minimum, even my phone plan. I'd also look into a practical route, like a licence in electrical or HVAC work, since hands-on lasts a few years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and driven. I'd work harder, not less, because that's how I deal with fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd look at an electrical or HVAC licence. Is that something you'd really consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My uncle does air conditioning and he never lacks work. It's not my dream, but I'm not too proud. A secure trade is better than a proud unemployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd tell me to save and keep my faith. They've lived through hard times in two countries, so they don't panic easily. They'd say keep studying while you can.

say: People should look after their **families**, neighbours and savings.
Businesses and government should work together so ordinary people don't carry all the **risk**.
think: My whole field is the **first thing** AGI does, and I have no savings.
I might finish a **degree** that isn't worth much, and my clients might not need me.
do: Use AI to **earn** as much as possible now and save most of it.
Look into an **electrical or HVAC** licence, since hands-on lasts longer.
feel: **Scared** and driven, because I work harder when I'm afraid.
S2.quote: A secure trade is better than a proud unemployment.
fieldNote: She is willing to **drop pride** for a secure trade.
Her **parents'** hard history makes her steady under pressure.
Her reaction to fear is **more work**, a sign of her adaptive style.

steps.text: Sell AI-built automations to local shops while demand lasts
Cut spending to rent, food and travel only
Ask my uncle about an air conditioning apprenticeship
Save most of every payment in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is real time, and people should use it. I'd tell friends to get a skill, a bit of money behind them and a small network. I'd also say that employers should offer apprenticeships and not just ask for experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel reasonably good. I'd graduate in 2029 with four years of AI experience and a portfolio of real clients, which is a strong start. When AGI arrives in 2031, I'd be someone who already works with it. Robots in 2034 could matter for my garden centre job, but I'd have moved on by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and turn my freelance work into a small company by third year. I'd register it properly, keep my accounts straight and look for steady monthly clients. I'd save at least 100 a month, and I'd find a mentor in the enterprise society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a bit of nerves. I like having a clear window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the company actually sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reliable small-business tech for shops, clinics and community groups. Websites, bookings, simple data tools, support when something breaks. Folks pay for someone who answers the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big firms could offer the same thing cheaper through AGI, and my clients would just use that. Then I'd need a trade or a job with a firm. I'd keep that exit ready, just in case.

say: Five years is real time, so get a **skill**, some money and a small network.
Employers should offer **apprenticeships**, not just ask for experience.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with a **portfolio** of real clients, a strong start.
By 2031 I'd already be someone who **works with** AGI.
do: Turn freelance work into a registered **small company** by third year.
**Save** at least 100 a month and find a mentor in the enterprise society.
feel: **Optimistic** with a bit of nerves, because I like a clear window.
S3.quote: Folks pay for someone who answers the phone.
fieldNote: She builds a **company** plan from what she does now.
She keeps a **trade exit** ready, which shows realistic thinking.
Her **optimism** depends on keeping a few years of lead.

steps.text: Register my freelance work as a small company
Save 100 a month toward a cushion
Find a mentor through the enterprise society

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and anyone willing to work can find a path. I'd say people should build something of their own and keep their community close. I'd also say we should expect governments to help those who really can't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel optimistic. By 2036 I'd be 28, with a business, savings and maybe a family. I'd have time to try things and fail safely. Robots come around 2039, and I'd already be thinking about what they mean for the garden centre and my uncle's trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, grow the business with a couple of employees and invest in a place of my own. I'd keep learning the newest tools every year, and I'd set aside money for my parents. I'd also volunteer teaching coding to kids at my mosque, since that's how I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ambitious. This is the picture I like best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think would trouble you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairness, mostly. I've had the push to learn this stuff, but not everybody has that. I'd like the gains to reach people who work with their hands too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this differ from the 2031 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Runway. Five years is a sprint with a plan. Ten gives me room to try a second idea if the first one fails.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, so anyone willing to work can find a path.
Governments should help those who really **can't adapt**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with a **business**, savings and maybe a family.
Robots come around **2039**, and I'd think about my uncle's trade.
do: **Grow** the business with a couple of employees and invest in a home.
**Teach** coding to kids at my mosque as a volunteer.
feel: **Calm** and ambitious, and this is the picture I like best.
S4.quote: Five years is a sprint with a plan. Ten gives me room to try a second idea if the first one fails.
fieldNote: Only the **ten-year** world gives her room to fail safely.
She links her success to **fairness** for people who work with their hands.
She wants to **give back** by teaching coding where she started.

steps.text: Hire two part-time staff as the business grows
Save toward a deposit on a small home
Teach coding to children at the mosque on weekends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have no savings and my whole field would be first in line. What would help is a short-term safety net, like paid retraining, and a clear route into a trade without huge costs. And honest advice about which jobs to avoid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask where I get my drive from. My parents arrived with two suitcases, and they never complained. I tell myself I can handle a lot more than I think. I remember that whenever things feel scary.

headlineQuote: My parents arrived with two suitcases, and they never complained. I tell myself I can handle a lot more than I think.
portrait: Vera is 18, studies **computing**, rents a room and builds websites for community clients beside weekend garden centre work.
She is traditional, favours **effort** over handouts, and uses AI tools every day to move quickly.
Thin money keeps her **uneasy** in most worlds, and anxious if AGI arrives by 2028.
Her fallback is a **hands-on trade** through her uncle, and her hope is a small company.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, with no savings and her field first in line.
whatWouldHelp: A short-term **safety net** like paid retraining and a cheap route into a trade.
Honest advice about which **jobs** to avoid.
